claims.text: Mechanical alloying can incorporate a uniform dispersion of nanoscale oxide particles into a high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Nanoscale oxide particles hinder dislocation motion in the alloy matrix.
Nanoscale oxide particles pin grain boundaries in the alloy matrix.
Hindering dislocation motion improves the mechanical strength and durability of the alloy.
Dislocation obstruction and grain-boundary pinning improve room-temperature creep resistance.
Dispersed oxide particles contribute to the formation of a passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer enhances corrosion resistance.
The oxide-dispersion-treated alloy will have greater mechanical durability than the untreated alloy.
The oxide-dispersion-treated alloy will have a lower room-temperature creep rate than the untreated alloy.
The oxide-dispersion-treated alloy will have greater corrosion resistance than the untreated alloy.
The predicted improvements should hold at room temperature under ambient atmospheric conditions and moderate moisture exposure.
Achieving the predicted improvements depends on obtaining a homogeneous oxide-particle distribution.
Significant oxide-particle agglomeration may negate the predicted improvements.
Incompatible alloy chemistries may negate the predicted improvements.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with processing parameters and alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome asserts improvement in all three properties, but the falsification rule permits the hypothesis to survive when only two properties improve. Thus, a failure of one explicitly predicted outcome would not falsify the full hypothesis.
